title: Subject pronouns (je, tu, il/elle, on, nous, vous, ils/elles)
explanation: French verbs almost always need a stated subject pronoun (unlike Spanish/Italian, which drop it). On is a chameleon meaning "we" (colloquial), "one," or "people/they."
bridge_note: French eroded its Latin verb endings phonetically (many now sound identical — parle/parles/parlent are all /paʁl/), so the pronoun became obligatory to mark person. English did the same thing centuries earlier for the same reason.
mistake: dropping the subject ("Suis fatigué" ✗ → "Je suis fatigué" ✓); using tu to a stranger (see Unit 14).
source: Eaquals tags "pronoms personnels sujets" at A1

title: Basic word order (SVO) and the "no do-support" rule
explanation: French is Subject–Verb–Object like English, but has no auxiliary "do." Questions and negations don't insert a helper verb.

examples.gloss: I eat / am eating an apple.

mistake: English speakers over-apply "do/does/did" ("Est-ce que tu fais aimer..." ✗). Also, French has no continuous "am ...-ing" tense — je mange covers both "I eat" and "I am eating."

title: être (to be) — present
explanation: être ('to be') is a core irregular verb (je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont) used for identity, nationality, profession, and location. Unlike English, no article appears before an unmodified profession (je suis étudiant, not je suis un étudiant).

examples.gloss: I am a student. (note: no article before an unmodified profession)

bridge_note: French collapses "to be" into a single verb, but Portuguese splits it into ser (identity, profession, characteristics) and estar (temporary states, location) — so je suis étudiant maps to sou estudante (ser) while nous sommes en France maps to estamos na França (estar), a distinction French speakers must learn to make.
mistake: inserting un/une before a bare profession ("Je suis un étudiant" is marked/emphatic, not the default).

title: avoir (to have) — present, and its idioms
explanation: Where English uses "to be" for states, French often uses avoir: age, hunger, fear.

examples.gloss: I am twenty (literal: I have twenty years).
She is hungry (literal: she has hunger).

bridge_note: Latin used habere ("have") for such states; French kept the pattern, English shifted to "be."
mistake: "Je suis 20 ans" ✗ / "Je suis faim" ✗.

title: c'est vs il/elle est
explanation: C'est + article/name ("it's a...", "it's [name]"); il/elle est + bare adjective or profession.

examples.native: C'est un médecin. / Il est médecin.

mistake: "Il est un médecin" ✗ (must be either c'est un médecin or il est médecin).

title: Grammatical gender of nouns
explanation: Every noun is masculine or feminine, including inanimate objects (le livre = the book, la table = the table). Word endings are a strong predictor: per Roy Lyster's 2006 corpus analysis of 9,961 nouns in Le Robert Junior Illustré (published in Journal of French Language Studies 16, Cambridge University Press), "81 per cent of all feminine nouns and 80 per cent of all masculine nouns in the corpus are rule governed, having endings that systematically predict their gender." Endings in -tion/-té/-ette/-ence tend feminine; -age/-ment/-eau/-isme tend masculine.
long_form:
The first thing to unlearn about French gender is the idea that it's about sex. Le livre isn't masculine because books are somehow male, any more than la table is feminine because tables are somehow female — grammatical gender is a formal classification system, a set of noun "boxes" that happens to be labeled masculine and feminine, and every noun has to live in one of the two boxes whether or not it names a living thing. What makes the system learnable rather than arbitrary is that the boxes correlate strongly with word endings: Lyster's corpus study found roughly four in five nouns rule-governed by their ending alone, which means fluent gender intuition in French is much closer to a spelling pattern you absorb than a fact you memorize noun by noun.

Why two boxes, and why does French default to masculine when in doubt? Latin actually had three genders — masculine, feminine, and neuter — and French descends from Vulgar Latin's slow erosion of case and gender marking. As Latin's neuter nouns lost their distinct endings, most of them were reassigned to the masculine class, which is the direct historical reason masculine functions as French's "unmarked" or default gender today (in mixed-gender groups, in impersonal constructions, in borrowed and new words). Traces of the old neuter occasionally surface as genuine oddities: a word like amour is masculine in the singular (un grand amour) but can take feminine agreement in the literary plural (de folles amours) — a fossil of an intermediate stage in the collapse, not a rule anyone applies consciously anymore.

English went through its own, more radical version of this collapse: Old English had a full three-gender system much like Latin's, assigning gender to inanimate nouns exactly as French still does, but it was lost almost entirely during the Middle English period, leaving only "natural" gender (he/she for people and some animals, it for everything else). So an English speaker isn't approaching French gender from some entirely alien mental category — English simply gave up a system French kept. Portuguese, by contrast, preserved the same two-gender Latin-derived architecture as French, which is why the two languages line up on so many cognates (informação/l'information, both feminine) — but the correlation isn't guaranteed, and cognate nouns can and do carry different genders in the two languages, so a Lusophone learner has to resist the reflex of assuming gender transfers automatically just because the word does.

The most persistent mistakes come from exactly this instinct to import a rule from somewhere else — treating inanimate gender as arbitrary noise not worth learning systematically (the English-speaker's trap), or assuming a cognate keeps its home-language gender (the bridge-language trap). A subtler nuance sits on top of the ending-based rules: a small set of French words change meaning depending on which gender you give them — le mode (method/mood, grammatical) versus la mode (fashion); le tour (a turn, a trick) versus la tour (a tower); le critique (the critic, the person) versus la critique (the criticism, the review). These aren't exceptions to "real" gender rules so much as proof that gender in French is doing genuine semantic work, distinguishing otherwise-identical words — which is also exactly why contemporary debates over écriture inclusive (inclusive writing) are as fraught as they are: they're proposing to modify a grammatical system that, unlike in English, touches nearly every sentence a French speaker produces.
bridge_note: French inherited Latin's masculine/feminine but lost Latin's neuter, folding most neuters into the masculine. That's why the "default"/unmarked gender is masculine.
mistake: assuming inanimate = neuter (English habit); assuming a word is masculine because its referent is (la personne, la victime are always feminine; le professeur historically masculine).

title: Plural of nouns (-s, -x, -aux)
explanation: Most add silent -s; nouns in -eau/-eu add -x; many in -al → -aux.
bridge_note: the -x plural is a medieval scribal abbreviation for "-us" that fossilized into spelling.
mistake: pronouncing the plural -s; forgetting the -al/-aux switch.

title: The agreement principle (overview)
explanation: Introduce the concept early: determiners and adjectives copy the noun's gender and number. This is the single organizing idea behind Units 3 and 4.

title: Definite articles (le, la, l', les)
explanation: "The," but also used for general/abstract statements where English uses no article.
mistake: omitting the article in generalizations ("J'aime chocolat" ✗).

title: Indefinite articles (un, une, des)
explanation: "A/an"; des = "some" (plural), which English usually drops.
mistake: dropping des ("J'ai amis" ✗).

title: Partitive articles (du, de la, de l', des)
explanation: "Some/any" of an uncountable mass. Contrast with definite: j'aime le café (coffee in general) vs je bois du café (some coffee).
long_form:
The partitive is one of French's most genuinely original contributions to Romance grammar, and it's worth pausing on why it exists at all. Latin had no articles whatsoever — no le, no un, no du — so a Roman speaker distinguished "I like coffee in general" from "I'm drinking some coffee" purely through context and word choice, not through a dedicated grammatical marker. French built its entire article system from scratch during the medieval period, recruiting the Latin demonstrative ille/illa ("that") to become le/la, the numeral unus/una to become un/une, and — this is the interesting part — the preposition de ("of, from") plus the definite article to build a brand-new category: du, de la, de l', literally "of the." The partitive names an unmeasured slice of a mass or category by describing it as a portion drawn "from the" whole, which is exactly what je bois du café means if you unpack it literally: "I drink [some] of the coffee."

That literal transparency is also why the definite/partitive contrast feels so sharp once you see it: j'aime le café talks about coffee as a category or an abstraction (the whole "the" that du later carves a piece out of), while je bois du café talks about an actual, physical, unspecified quantity of it sitting in a cup. English speakers don't have a real equivalent decision to make here, because English simply doesn't require an article at all for this meaning — "I drink coffee" and "I'm drinking some coffee" are both grammatical, and "some" is optional, stylistic, almost always droppable. That optionality is precisely the trap: English gives learners no formal signal that a choice is even being made, so the instinct is to treat du/de la as decorative rather than structurally required.

Portuguese complicates the transfer in the opposite direction from English. Portuguese, like French, descends from Latin and built its own indefinite plural (uns, umas) and occasionally uses de-constructions for partitive-like meaning, but it does not have an obligatory partitive article the way French does — Como pão ("I eat bread") is perfectly natural and complete without any word corresponding to du. So a Lusophone learner approaching French partitives isn't transferring a habit from Portuguese so much as acquiring a genuinely new obligatory category that neither of their languages forces on them the same way — which makes this one of the harder points in the whole curriculum to get by instinct, no matter which side of the bridge you're coming from.

The deepest A2-level trap, as the curriculum note says, is using the definite where the partitive belongs and vice versa — but the more interesting nuance for an intermediate learner is that abstract nouns don't behave uniformly. Some abstractions default to the definite because French treats them as named, whole concepts (aimer la liberté, respecter la nature), while others regularly take the partitive because French treats them as a variable quantity someone can have more or less of on a given occasion (avoir du courage, avoir de la patience, avoir de la chance) — the same noun, courage, can appear with le when discussed as a virtue in the abstract and with du when describing how much of it someone is currently displaying. Getting a feel for that line is less about memorizing a list and more about learning to ask, every time: am I naming the whole category, or scooping out an unmeasured piece of it?

examples.native: Je mange du pain et de la confiture.

bridge_note: the partitive is a contraction of de + definite article ("of the"), literally "some of the." It marks an unmeasured portion.
mistake: the deepest A2 trap — using the definite where the partitive is needed, and vice versa.
source: Eaquals; the du/le distinction tagged A2

title: Articles become "de" after negation and quantity
explanation: Indefinite and partitive articles collapse to bare de after a negative or an expression of quantity. Definite articles do NOT change; and after être the article stays.

examples.native: Je mange des pommes. → Je ne mange pas de pommes.
beaucoup de vin, un litre d'eau
examples.gloss: a lot of wine, a litre of water.

examples.native: BUT: Ce n'est pas un problème.
examples.gloss: It's not a problem (être keeps un).

mistake: "Je ne mange pas des pommes" ✗; reducing after être.

title: Contractions: à + le = au, de + le = du (au/aux/du/des)
explanation: Obligatory fusion; à la and à l' do NOT contract.
mistake: "à le cinéma" ✗, "de le garage" ✗.

title: Demonstrative adjectives (ce, cet, cette, ces)
explanation: "This/that/these/those." Cet before a masculine vowel/mute-h word. Add -ci/-là to disambiguate this vs that.

examples.native: ce livre, cet homme, cette femme, ces enfants
Je préfère cette robe-ci à cette robe-là.
examples.gloss: I prefer this dress to that dress.

title: Possessive adjectives (mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses, notre/votre/leur…)
explanation: They agree with the thing possessed, not the possessor — so son/sa means "his" OR "her," decided by the noun's gender.

examples.native: son livre = his/her book; sa voiture = his/her car
Ma → mon before a feminine noun starting with a vowel: mon amie

bridge_note: Latin possessives agreed with the possessed noun; French kept this, so gender is grammatical, not referential.
mistake: the single biggest error — choosing the possessive by the owner's sex ("sa" for "his" only). Also "ma amie" ✗ → mon amie.

title: Adjective agreement (gender + number)
explanation: Default: add -e for feminine, -s for plural. Many irregular feminines (-eux→-euse, -f→-ve, -er→-ère).

examples.native: un petit chat / une petite chatte / des petits chats
un homme heureux / une femme heureuse

mistake: leaving the adjective invariable (English habit).

title: Adjective placement: the BANGS/BAGS exception
explanation: Most adjectives FOLLOW the noun (une voiture rouge). A small high-frequency set precedes it: Beauty, Age, Numbers, Goodness, Size (beau, jeune/vieux, premier, bon/mauvais, grand/petit).
long_form:
The default rule — adjectives follow the noun — is itself the more interesting historical fact, because it's the opposite of what English speakers expect from any language and yet it's the ordinary Romance pattern: Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese all put descriptive adjectives after the noun by default too. What actually needs explaining isn't why French postposes adjectives; it's why a small cluster of them refuses to. The BANGS/BAGS set — beauty, age, number, goodness, size — isn't a random grab bag someone assembled for a mnemonic. It's a genuine linguistic pattern: cross-linguistically, the adjectives most likely to sit in a fixed, unusual position next to a noun tend to be exactly the short, extremely frequent, semantically "inherent" ones — words so old and so constantly used that they behave more like part of the noun phrase's core than like an added description, the way English still says "a big deal" rather than "a deal big" even though English adjectives are otherwise always prenominal anyway.

Historically, Latin word order was far freer than French's, because Latin's case endings did the job that word order does in French — you could tell subject from object from the endings, not the position, so an adjective could sit almost anywhere for stylistic or emphatic effect. As French lost virtually all of its case marking and locked into a strict word-order grammar to compensate, adjective position had to be fixed too — and the pattern that emerged split along frequency lines: the oldest, shortest, most habitually paired adjective-noun combinations (grand-mère, petit-déjeuner, bon vin) fossilized in their inherited front position, while the much larger and more productive class of descriptive adjectives — colors, shapes, nationalities, textures, anything coined or borrowed more recently — settled into the newer, more "regular" post-nominal slot.

For an English speaker this is one of the more disorienting asymmetries in French, precisely because English never made this split: every English adjective goes before its noun, full stop, so there's no internal category to map BANGS onto. Portuguese offers a genuinely useful comparison instead of a false-friend trap here, because Portuguese preserves an almost parallel phenomenon with its own small set of frequently-preposed adjectives (grande, bom, mau, velho, novo) — grande homem (a great man) versus homem grande (a big/tall man) works on exactly the same logic as French's own position-sensitive adjectives, so a Lusophone learner already has the right mental category, just not the identical membership list.

The most common mistake isn't just picking the wrong side for an individual adjective — it's treating the whole rule as either universal (postposing everything, the safe English-speaker's overcorrection) or as freely stylistic (front-loading adjectives at will, mistaking BANGS for a suggestion rather than a fixed lexical fact about specific words). The genuinely useful nuance, and the bridge to the next point in this unit, is that BANGS membership isn't airtight even within itself: grand can sit in front for a qualitative, non-literal sense (un grand homme, a great man) and behind for a literal, physical one (un homme grand, a tall man) — which is really adjectives-that-change-meaning-by-position showing up early, a preview that placement in French is never just decorative; it's carrying real, sometimes subtle, semantic weight.
bridge_note: the pre-posed set is the oldest, most frequent, most "inherent-quality" adjective group — frequency entrenched their Latin-era front position while newer/descriptive adjectives took the analytic post-position.
mistake: placing all adjectives after ("une rouge voiture" ✗) or all before.

title: Adjectives that change meaning by position
explanation: ancien (former/old), cher (dear/expensive), propre (own/clean), grand (great/tall), dernier (last-in-series/previous).

examples.native: mon ancien appartement (my former flat) vs un meuble ancien (an antique)
un cher ami vs une robe chère
examples.gloss: a dear friend vs an expensive dress

mistake: assuming position is free.

title: Comparatives (plus/moins/aussi … que)
explanation: Comparisons use plus/moins/aussi before the adjective and que after it ("more/less/as … as"), and the adjective still agrees with the noun as it normally would. bon and bien are irregular: they become meilleur (adjective) and mieux (adverb) instead of plus bon / plus bien.

examples.native: Elle est plus grande que moi.
Il court aussi vite que toi.
examples.gloss: He runs as fast as you.

mistake: "plus bon" ✗ → meilleur; confusing meilleur (adj.) with mieux (adv.).

title: Superlatives (le plus / le moins …)
explanation: The superlative is the comparative with a definite article added (le/la/les plus/moins + adjective), so it agrees with the noun in gender and number the same way. When ranking within a place or group, French uses de ("in/of") after the superlative rather than dans.

examples.native: C'est le restaurant le plus cher de la ville.
examples.gloss: It's the most expensive restaurant in the city.

mistake: using dans instead of de for "in" after a superlative ("le plus cher dans la ville" ✗).

title: Regular -er verbs (présent)
explanation: parler: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent. The first conjugation (-er, except aller) contains roughly 6,000 verbs and is the only class still productive — new coinages join it (téléviser, atomiser, googliser), whereas the -ir group has only about 300 verbs.

examples.native: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent
examples.gloss: I speak, you speak, he speaks, we speak, you speak, they speak (parler = to speak)

mistake: pronouncing -ent (it is silent).
source: Eaquals A1; the largest, most productive class

title: Regular -ir verbs (finir type) and -re verbs (vendre type)
explanation: finir: je finis … nous finissons (note the -iss- infix). vendre: je vends, il vend (no ending in 3sg).

examples.native: je finis, nous finissons / je vends, il vend
examples.gloss: I finish, we finish / I sell, he sells

mistake: forgetting -iss- in the plural; adding an ending to il vend.

title: Key irregular verbs: aller, faire, venir, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, savoir
explanation: High-frequency and each anchors later constructions (aller→futur proche; venir→passé récent; pouvoir/vouloir/devoir = modals).

examples.native: Je vais, tu fais, il vient, nous pouvons, ils veulent

title: Reflexive/pronominal verbs (se laver, se lever)
explanation: The subject acts on itself; the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous/se) sits before the verb.
long_form:
Calling se laver and se lever "reflexive" undersells how much work this one pronoun does in French. A true reflexive — the subject acting on itself, like washing oneself — is really just one job among several that the se-construction handles. There's the reciprocal use (ils se parlent, "they talk to each other," where two or more subjects act on each other rather than themselves); there's a broad class of verbs that are pronominal by nature and have no independent non-reflexive meaning at all (se souvenir, "to remember," doesn't mean anything as a bare verb *souvenir); and there's a generic, agentless use covered elsewhere in this curriculum (le vin se boit frais) that shades into something closer to a passive. One small grammatical device, several distinct jobs — which is the hallmark of what linguists call a grammaticalized marker, a form that started narrow and widened its coverage over time.

That widening has a real historical source: Latin had a genuine middle voice, partly preserved through a set of "deponent" verbs (passive in form but active in meaning) and partly expressed with a reflexive pronoun for actions where the subject is affected by its own action without a separate object being acted upon. French's se-verbs are the direct continuation of that Latin reflexive/middle system, and the "inherently pronominal" verbs with no independent meaning — se souvenir, se moquer de, se plaindre, s'en aller — are effectively living fossils of Latin deponents: verbs whose grammatical form is reflexive but whose actual meaning has drifted so far from literal self-action that a learner has to just memorize them as vocabulary, the reflexive pronoun functioning as an inseparable part of the verb rather than as a meaningful "self" anymore.

English never grammaticalized a middle voice at all — it either uses a genuine reflexive pronoun only when the reflexivity needs to be made explicit and would otherwise be ambiguous ("he shaved himself," as opposed to the far more common "he shaved," which is understood as reflexive by default with no pronoun at all), or it reaches for a completely different strategy, the "get"-passive ("the door got stuck") or a plain intransitive ("the door opened"), to express the same middle-voice meaning of a subject undergoing rather than performing an action. Portuguese, by contrast, inherited essentially the same se-system directly and in parallel with French — se lavar, se lembrar, se queixar de map almost verb-for-verb onto their French cousins — making this one of the more reliably transferable points in the entire curriculum for a learner coming from Portuguese, with the caveat that everyday spoken Portuguese sometimes drops the reflexive pronoun more casually with body-care verbs than formal French ever allows.

The most common learner mistakes both stem from treating se as optional decoration rather than a grammatical requirement that changes meaning: omitting it turns a reflexive verb into an entirely different, usually transitive, verb (je lève means "I lift [something else]"; je me lève means "I get [myself] up"), and getting the pronoun's person wrong (using se instead of me/te with a first- or second-person subject) breaks the agreement the construction depends on. The deeper nuance worth sitting with is that you can't reliably predict from a verb's English translation whether French will require se — "I remember" has no reflexive shape in English at all, so nothing in the English sentence warns a learner that se souvenir needs one, which is exactly why these verbs have to be learned as fixed lexical units, se and all, rather than derived on the fly from a general reflexivity rule.

examples.native: Je me lève à sept heures.

bridge_note: many "reflexives" are really middle-voice (se souvenir = to remember) — a Latin deponent/middle relic where the action folds back on the subject.
mistake: omitting the reflexive ("Je lève" = I lift [something else]); wrong pronoun agreement.

title: Modal + infinitive (pouvoir/vouloir/devoir/savoir + inf.)
explanation: The modals pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, and savoir are followed directly by a bare infinitive with no linking preposition, and that second verb never conjugates, no matter who the subject is.

examples.native: Je peux venir. Je veux partir. Je dois travailler. Je sais nager

mistake: conjugating the second verb ("Je peux viens" ✗ → infinitive).

title: Futur proche (aller + infinitive)
explanation: "Going to" future.

title: Passé récent (venir de + infinitive)
explanation: "To have just done."
mistake: using passé composé instead ("J'ai juste fini" is an anglicism).

title: Present progressive (être en train de + infinitive)
explanation: Emphasizes action in progress — used far less than English "-ing."

examples.native: Je suis en train de cuisiner.

mistake: over-using it as a default present (the French present already covers "-ing").

title: Impératif (commands)
explanation: Drop the subject; -er verbs drop the -s in the tu form (Mange! Parle!). Irregular: sois/aie/sache.
mistake: keeping the subject; pronoun order in affirmative commands (see 8.6).

title: ne … pas
explanation: The verb sits inside the clamp; in compound tenses the clamp wraps the auxiliary.
long_form:
French negation looks like a two-part "clamp" around the verb because it is, quite literally, a snapshot of a language-change process caught in mid-transition — a pattern the Danish linguist Otto Jespersen described so thoroughly across so many languages that it now bears his name, Jespersen's Cycle. The cycle runs like this: a plain negator erodes phonetically over time until it's weak and easy to miss in speech, so speakers start reinforcing it with some emphatic word for extra force; that reinforcing word gets used so constantly that it stops feeling emphatic and becomes just part of ordinary negation; eventually the original negator can be dropped entirely, leaving the former reinforcement to carry the whole job alone — at which point the cycle is free to start again with some new intensifier.

French is presently living through two stages of exactly this cycle at once. The original Latin negator non became French's ne, which by the medieval period had already worn down phonetically (in casual speech today it's often reduced to barely a vowel, or dropped in writing as n'). To compensate, French speakers began reinforcing ne with concrete nouns for emphasis, the way English still says "I don't care one bit" or "I didn't sleep a wink" — French tried several of these: pas ("a step," used with verbs of motion, "not walk a step"), goutte ("a drop," with boire, "drink"), mie ("a crumb," with manger, "eat"). Pas simply won the competition and generalized to all verbs, losing its literal "step" meaning entirely along the way — which is why modern French genuinely negates with two words, ne and pas, that jointly clamp the verb. And right now, in casual spoken French, the cycle is quietly completing its next lap: ne is being dropped (je sais pas), leaving pas alone to do what ne used to do by itself, exactly the fate that originally befell non.

English underwent the identical cycle centuries earlier and simply finished it: Old English ne was reinforced by naht/nawiht ("no thing," the ancestor of "not"), that reinforcement became obligatory, and eventually ne dropped out altogether, leaving modern English with a single-word negator, not, that nobody perceives as a reinforcement anymore because its origin as a noun ("thing") has been completely forgotten. So an English speaker hearing colloquial French drop ne isn't watching some alien erosion of grammar — they're watching French catch up to a step English took hundreds of years ago, just via a different reinforcing word. Portuguese, notably, never developed this two-part system at all; não has functioned as a single, stable negator throughout its documented history, which means this entire cyclical story is a genuinely French-specific complication with nothing to transfer from the bridge language — if anything, a Lusophone learner has to actively acquire an unfamiliar structural habit rather than lean on an existing one.

The practical upshot for a learner is that dropping ne isn't sloppiness to be corrected out of a student — it's the expected, productive form in casual registers, and treating it as an error misses what's actually going on; the real skill is controlling both ends of an ongoing sound change, keeping ne in writing and formal speech while allowing it to disappear in relaxed conversation. The more mechanical trap is placing pas in the wrong slot in compound tenses: because the clamp wraps whichever verb is conjugated, pas sits after the auxiliary and before the participle (je n'ai pas mangé), not after the participle the way an English speaker instinctively wants to append a negator at the end ("I have not eaten" tempts "j'ai mangé pas," which is simply ungrammatical) — a reminder that the clamp isn't wrapping "the verb" loosely but very specifically the finite, conjugated form.
bridge_note: ne was the original Latin negator (non); pas ("step") was an intensifier ("not a step") that got reanalyzed as the real negative — which is why colloquial French now drops ne and keeps pas.
mistake: dropping ne (fine in casual speech — "je sais pas" — but flag as register, Unit 14); placing pas after the participle ("Je n'ai mangé pas" ✗).

title: ne … jamais / rien / personne / plus
explanation: never / nothing / nobody / no longer.
mistake: personne and rien as subjects invert ("Personne ne vient" — nobody's coming); double-translating ("Je ne veux pas rien" ✗).
source: Eaquals sequences jamais at A1, plus/personne/rien at A2

title: ne … que (restrictive "only")
explanation: Not a true negative — it restricts. que precedes the restricted element.
bridge_note: ne…que = "nothing except," a fossilized comparative-exceptive; that's why it doesn't trigger the de-reduction that real negatives do.
mistake: treating it as negative and reducing the article ("Je n'ai que de dix euros" ✗ — after ne…que the normal article stays: Je ne bois que du vin).

title: ne … aucun, ni … ni
explanation: ne … aucun is a stronger, more emphatic "no/none whatsoever" than ne … pas de, and aucun(e) agrees in gender with the noun it modifies. ne … ni … ni negates two or more items in parallel ("neither … nor"), with ni placed directly before each negated item.

examples.native: Il ne mange ni viande ni poisson.
examples.gloss: He eats neither meat nor fish.

title: The three yes/no question strategies
explanation: (1) Intonation (casual): Tu viens ? (2) Est-ce que (neutral): Est-ce que tu viens ? (3) Inversion (formal): Viens-tu ?

examples.native: Tu viens ? / Est-ce que tu viens ? / Viens-tu ?
examples.gloss: Are you coming? — casual / neutral / formal

mistake: over-using inversion in speech (sounds stiff); forgetting the euphonic -t- (A-t-il ?).

title: Information words: qui, que/quoi, où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi, quel
explanation: These words slot into any of the three question strategies to ask for specific information rather than a yes/no answer. quel is an adjective that agrees with the noun it modifies, unlike the other, invariable words in this set.
mistake: quel (adjective, agrees) vs qu'est-ce que (pronoun); "Qu'est-ce que" vs "qui est-ce qui" for things vs people.

title: Qu'est-ce que c'est / Qu'est-ce qui / Qui est-ce que
explanation: The "long forms" that avoid inversion.
mistake: mixing the qui/que and subject/object slots.

title: lequel (which one) and inversion in compound tenses
explanation: lequel/laquelle/lesquels/lesquelles mean "which one(s)" and agree in gender and number with the noun they replace, letting a speaker single out an item from a known set. In an inversion question built on a compound tense, the subject pronoun attaches after the conjugated auxiliary, not after the past participle.

examples.gloss: Have you eaten? (inversion wraps the auxiliary).

title: Direct object pronouns (me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les)
explanation: Placed BEFORE the conjugated verb (unlike English, which puts objects after).
long_form:
French object pronouns going before the verb feels like an arbitrary quirk until you see it as the last visible remnant of a grammatical system French otherwise abandoned completely: case. Latin marked a noun's grammatical role — subject, direct object, indirect object — with endings (case suffixes) that let word order stay remarkably free, because the ending itself told you who did what to whom regardless of position. As spoken Latin evolved into Old French, those noun-case endings eroded away almost entirely, and word order hardened into the strict Subject-Verb-Object pattern French uses today to compensate. Pronouns, though, didn't go quietly: because they're short, extremely frequent, and phonologically light, they resisted the general erosion longer than full nouns did, and instead of losing their case distinctions they fossilized them into a fixed position — leaning (procliticizing, in the technical term) onto the verb they depend on, the way an unstressed syllable leans onto the stressed syllable next to it. That's the deep reason French still visibly distinguishes je (subject) from me (object) from moi (stressed/tonic) for the exact same first-person referent, long after French nouns lost every trace of case marking: pronouns are, cross-linguistically, always the last holdout of a dying case system, because they're the words a language's speakers use too often and too automatically to simplify away easily.

The clitic's fixed pre-verbal position is what actually produces the word-order clash English speakers feel most acutely: Je le vois literally reads "I him see" if you translate word for word, because English pronouns, unlike French ones, never fused onto the verb this way — English kept a vestige of pronoun case (I/me, he/him, they/them) but simply slotted it into the ordinary post-verbal object position that any noun would occupy, since English's word order rigidified around the verb-then-object pattern without ever developing a special pre-verbal parking spot for light pronouns the way French did. So the mismatch isn't really about pronouns at all — English and French agree that pronouns keep a form distinct from nouns — the mismatch is specifically about where that pronoun physically sits relative to the verb.

Portuguese makes the comparison genuinely illuminating rather than just confusing, because it shows that "clitic goes before or after the verb" is a real structural choice languages make differently, not a fixed law of Romance grammar. European Portuguese has a three-way system: enclisis (attaching after the verb, the unmarked default — vejo-o, "I see him"), proclisis (attaching before, triggered by negation, question words, and certain subordinating conjunctions — não o vejo), and even mesoclisis, where the clitic is inserted inside the verb itself in the future and conditional (vê-lo-ei, "I will see him"). French, by contrast, simplified this whole three-way system down to essentially one fixed rule: the clitic goes before the conjugated verb, full stop, with no default/triggered split. That means a French speaker's instinct to always front the pronoun is only sometimes right for Portuguese — correct for the triggered proclisis contexts, wrong for the far more common default enclitic case — while a Portuguese speaker learning French gets the easier end of the deal, since French never asks them to choose.

The classic beginner mistake is straightforward English-order substitution ("je vois le" for "I see him"), but the more durable trap shows up once modal or semi-auxiliary constructions enter the picture: the pronoun still has to attach to whichever verb it's logically the object of, not simply to "the verb" in some vague sense, which is why je veux le voir ("I want to see it," pronoun before the infinitive it belongs to) contrasts with constructions like the causative faire, where all pronoun objects front onto faire itself regardless of which embedded verb they logically belong to. And the whole fixed-position rule flips entirely in the affirmative imperative (Donne-le-moi!, pronoun after the verb, hyphenated) — not a contradiction so much as a separate historical layer, since the imperative in the Romance languages restructured its clitic placement independently of the ordinary declarative clause, a wrinkle worth knowing exists even before drilling the specific commands where it applies.
bridge_note: French lost noun case endings but kept the Latin rule that unstressed object pronouns lean (procliticize) onto the verb — hence they precede it. This is the deep reason French kept "pronoun cases" (me/te/le/lui) while abandoning noun cases.
mistake: English word order ("Je vois le" ✗).
branch: Object Pronouns, y/en, and Pronoun Ordering

title: Indirect object pronouns (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur)
explanation: Replace à + person. lui = to him/her; leur = to them.
mistake: confusing lui (indirect, to him/her) with le/la (direct); using leur + -s (it's invariable as a pronoun).

title: y (there / to it)
explanation: Replaces à + thing/place.
mistake: using y for people (use lui/leur).
branch: Object Pronouns, y/en, and Pronoun Ordering

title: en (some / of it / from there)
explanation: Replaces de + noun, and quantities.
mistake: dropping en where French requires the quantity resumption ("J'ai trois" ✗ when standing alone → J'en ai trois).
branch: Object Pronouns, y/en, and Pronoun Ordering

title: Double object pronoun ordering
explanation: Fixed order before the verb: me/te/se/nous/vous → le/la/les → lui/leur → y → en.
mistake: wrong internal order ("Je lui le donne" ✗).

title: Pronouns in affirmative commands
explanation: In positive commands pronouns follow the verb, hyphenated, and me/te → moi/toi.

title: Stress/tonic pronouns (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles)
explanation: After prepositions, for emphasis, and in c'est ….

examples.native: avec moi, chez eux; Moi, je pense que… ; C'est lui

mistake: using subject pronouns after prepositions ("avec je" ✗).

title: Passé composé with avoir
explanation: avoir (present) + past participle. Participles: -er→-é, -ir→-i, -re→-u, plus many irregulars (fait, pris, eu, été).
mistake: choosing the wrong auxiliary; irregular participles.
source: Eaquals tags p.c. with avoir at A1, with être at A2

title: Passé composé with être (the DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP verbs)
explanation: The standard "DR MRS VANDERTRAMP" mnemonic covers 16 intransitive motion/state-change verbs (aller, venir, naître, mourir, monter, descendre, rester, partir, arriver, entrer, sortir, tomber, retourner, rentrer, devenir, revenir) plus the reflexives — all conjugate with être, and the participle then agrees with the SUBJECT. Of these, only naître→né, mourir→mort, and venir→venu (and its regular compounds devenir→devenu, revenir→revenu) have irregular participles. Several — notably monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer, and passer (often tacked on as an informal 17th member of the list) — switch to avoir when used transitively with a direct object, with a shift in meaning: elle est descendue ("she went down") vs elle a descendu l'escalier ("she went/brought down the stairs").
long_form:
The DR MRS VANDERTRAMP list looks, on first encounter, like a random collection of verbs someone needed a mnemonic to memorize — but it isn't random at all, and seeing why is more useful than memorizing the acronym. Every verb on the list shares one property: its subject doesn't perform an action on something else, it undergoes a change of state or location itself. Aller, venir, monter, descendre, naître, mourir, tomber — in every case the grammatical subject is the thing changing, moving, appearing, or vanishing, not an agent acting on a separate target. Linguists call this class of verbs "unaccusative," and the label is doing real work: an unaccusative verb's subject behaves, underneath the syntax, more like the object of a transitive sentence than like a true agentive subject (compare "the door opened" — the door didn't do anything, it changed state — with "she opened the door," where she is a genuine agent). Because the subject of an unaccusative verb is playing an object-like role, French treats it the way it treats any object-like element: with agreement, the same way an adjective agrees with the noun it describes through a copula. Elle est allée literally patterns like a predicate adjective ("she is [in a state of] gone"), which is exactly why the participle takes -e for a feminine subject the way an adjective would.

This isn't a French idiosyncrasy; it's a well-documented pattern across the languages that historically had two auxiliaries to choose from. Italian preserves an essere/avere split along nearly identical lines, and earlier stages of German and Dutch made the same sein/haben distinction that modern standard German has since largely abandoned. All of these languages inherited (or independently developed) the insight that unaccusative, subject-affected verbs deserve grammatical treatment different from ordinary transitive, agent-driven ones — French's être-list is simply the version of that split that survived intact into the modern standard language.

English lost this auxiliary split completely — have now covers every verb regardless of unaccusativity — but it didn't lose it without leaving fossils behind. Older or more formal English still occasionally uses be + past participle for exactly this class of verb: "he is risen," "she is gone," "Christ is come" are all be-constructions, precisely the English cousins of French's être-perfect, preserved mainly in liturgical and archaic registers (the King James Bible is full of them) after the ordinary spoken language generalized to have everywhere else. Portuguese offers no such parallel at all: ter (with haver surviving only in fossilized or very formal contexts) has been Portuguese's sole compound-past auxiliary throughout its documented history, with no be-verb alternation ever developed for unaccusatives — so a Lusophone learner isn't transferring a habit here so much as acquiring an entirely new category that their own language never grammaticalized, which is precisely why the instinct to reach for a single all-purpose auxiliary (mirroring ter) is the most persistent error this point produces for that group of learners.

The mnemonic itself is a teaching artifact, not a fact about how native speakers store the list — nobody consciously recites DR MRS VANDERTRAMP while conjugating; the class simply is unaccusative and être-taking, full stop, in a fluent speaker's grammar. Two nuances repay attention once the basic list is solid. First, the reflexives (ils se sont levés) take être for a historically separate reason from the intransitive-motion verbs — an unrelated Latin-era convention about reflexive/middle-voice constructions generally taking a "be"-type auxiliary — which is why the mnemonic doesn't (and shouldn't) try to fold reflexives into the same explanatory story even though they end up using the same auxiliary. Second, several of the list's core verbs — monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer, and colloquially passer — genuinely switch camp when they pick up a direct object, because a direct object turns the unaccusative motion verb into an ordinary transitive one with a real agent (elle est descendue, she herself changed location, versus elle a descendu l'escalier, she acted on the stairs by bringing something down them) — the auxiliary switch is tracking the same underlying grammatical logic the whole list is built on, not contradicting it.

examples.gloss: She went. / Nous sommes arrivés. — We arrived.

bridge_note: the être-verbs describe change of state/location — their subject undergoes the action, so French treats it like a predicate adjective that agrees, mirroring the Latin/Romance "unaccusative" pattern.
mistake: using avoir with these ("Elle a allé" ✗); forgetting subject agreement; and for monter/descendre/sortir/rentrer, wrongly keeping être even when there's a direct object — these switch to avoir when transitive (j'ai monté les valises, not je suis monté les valises).

title: Past-participle agreement with a preceding direct object (avoir)
explanation: With avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object ONLY when that object comes before the verb.
long_form:
Of every rule in this curriculum, this is the one native French speakers themselves most often get wrong in casual writing — which is a useful fact to lead with, because it reframes the rule from "a trap for learners" to "a genuinely difficult piece of French grammar that even educated adults have to think about." The logic, once stated plainly, is orderly: with avoir, the participle behaves like an ordinary verb form (invariable) by default, EXCEPT when the direct object it belongs to has already been mentioned earlier in the sentence — a pronoun, or a relative pronoun standing in for a noun already named — in which case the participle retroactively agrees with that object the way an adjective would agree with a noun it describes. J'ai acheté les fleurs has no agreement because the object follows the verb; les fleurs que j'ai achetées agrees because fleurs was already named before achetées arrives.

There's a well-known story about where this rule comes from, worth repeating with the caveat that it's tradition rather than settled fact: French teachers and grammar histories often credit the Renaissance poet Clément Marot with formulating the principle for the court of King François I, reasoning that a participle can only "look back" and agree with an object whose gender and number are already known to the speaker at the moment of speaking — an object still to come hasn't been specified yet, so there's nothing for the participle to agree with. Whether or not the anecdote about Marot is literally accurate (it's often treated as at least partly legendary), it captures the rule's actual logic exactly, and more importantly it points to something true about how this rule entered the language: unlike most French grammar, which emerged organically from sound change and usage, this is a rule imposed by prescriptive grammarians during French's 16th–17th century codification, in the era when the Académie française and its predecessors were actively standardizing "correct" French — one of the relatively few places where a grammar committee, not centuries of unplanned drift, shaped the exact rule millions of French schoolchildren still drill today.

Neither English nor Portuguese has anything resembling this rule, which means there's no useful transfer available from either side of the bridge — if anything, both languages actively work against the instinct needed here. English past participles never inflect for gender or number under any circumstances ("the letters I wrote," never "wrote-s"), and Portuguese's ter-based compound past is similarly invariable regardless of where the object sits (as tenho comprado, "I have been buying," never changes for a preceding object). So a learner from either background is acquiring a genuinely new category, not adapting an existing one — a fair explanation for why this particular rule is flagged as the single most error-prone spelling convention in French even for native speakers.

The nuance that makes this rule stranger still is that it is, in a meaningful sense, invisible in speech. Many of the relevant feminine and plural participle endings are spelled differently but pronounced identically to the masculine singular — vu, vue, vus, vues are all /vy/, so a fluent speaker saying les fleurs que j'ai vues aloud produces exactly the same sounds whether or not they're "getting the agreement right." (A smaller set, like pris/prise or fait/faite, does audibly change.) That means this is one of the rare corners of French grammar preserved almost entirely for the eye rather than the ear — a spelling convention with real orthographic consequences on a dictée or in formal writing, but close to undetectable in ordinary conversation, which is exactly why even native speakers who speak flawlessly can stumble on it the moment they pick up a pen.

examples.gloss: The flowers I bought (achetées agrees with fleurs, which precedes).

examples.native: BUT: J'ai acheté les fleurs (no agreement)

mistake: the single most error-prone spelling rule in French; agreeing with a following object.

title: Imparfait (formation and core uses)
explanation: Stem from the nous form + -ais/-ais/-ait/-ions/-iez/-aient. Uses: ongoing/background action, habits, description, states.

examples.gloss: It was raining and I was cold.

examples.native: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais au foot.
examples.gloss: When I was little, I used to play football.

mistake: mapping it one-to-one onto English past (it covers "was ...-ing," "used to," and descriptive "was").

title: Passé composé vs imparfait (the aspect contrast)
explanation: PC = completed, bounded events (foreground); imparfait = ongoing/repeated/descriptive (background). One often interrupts the other.
long_form:
The passé composé/imparfait contrast is the single point in this entire curriculum where English grammar simply offers no equivalent category to lean on, and it's worth being precise about why. Tense answers the question "when did this happen" (past, present, future); aspect answers a different question entirely — "how is this event structured internally: as a completed whole, or as something ongoing, repeated, or in the background?" English marks tense obligatorily but treats aspect as mostly optional and periphrastic (the choice between "it rained" and "it was raining" exists, but nothing forces an English speaker to choose one over the other the way French forces a choice between a plu and pleuvait every single time a past event is described). French, like Latin before it, grammaticalizes aspect as a genuinely obligatory category: you cannot describe a past event in French without simultaneously committing to whether you're presenting it as bounded/completed (passé composé) or as ongoing/habitual/descriptive background (imparfait).

That obligatory split is a direct continuation of Latin's own perfect/imperfect verb stems, which is real historical continuity — but the passé composé itself is not the direct descendant of the Latin perfect in form. That role actually belongs to the passé simple (the literary past covered elsewhere in this unit), a synthetic, one-word tense that continues Latin's perfect morphology in a fairly straight line. The passé composé is a French innovation: a newer, compound formation (avoir/être + participle) that gradually took over the everyday, spoken job of narrating completed past events, pushing the older synthetic passé simple into an increasingly literary and eventually purely written register. So French actually renewed the machinery expressing the perfective aspect while preserving the aspectual distinction itself essentially unchanged from Latin — the concept is ancient, the tool that carries it in speech is comparatively recent.

For an English speaker, the honest way to build intuition is to notice that English already makes exactly this same kind of distinction, just optionally and unconsciously, with "was ...-ing": "I was eating when the phone rang" already separates a backgrounded, ongoing action from a foregrounded, completed one, using almost the same logic French grammaticalizes with imparfait versus passé composé — the difference is that English lets you skip the distinction ("I ate when the phone rang" is also fine and means something close enough), while French simply never lets you skip it. Portuguese, by contrast, draws the identical line with the identical values using its own pretérito perfeito and pretérito imperfeito, which means a Lusophone learner isn't building a new mental category at all — the conceptual work is already done, and the task reduces to learning which French verb forms map onto which side of a distinction they already feel natively, one of the most direct and complete transfer points anywhere in this curriculum.

The genuinely advanced nuance — the one that separates a B1 learner drilling the rule from a fluent speaker using it — is that the "correct" choice between passé composé and imparfait isn't always dictated by the objective facts of what happened; it's dictated by how the speaker chooses to frame the event within a narrative. Il pleuvait ("it was raining," background, ongoing) and il a plu ("it rained," a completed event in the story's timeline) can, in principle, both be said of literally the same rainfall — the difference is whether the speaker is treating the rain as scenery the story happens against, or as an event that itself moves the story forward. That's not a fact about the weather; it's a narrative choice, and it's exactly why two native speakers can describe the same afternoon using different aspectual choices and both be entirely correct while meaning subtly different things.

examples.native: Je regardais la télé quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.gloss: I was watching TV when the phone rang.

bridge_note: French grammaticalizes aspect (bounded vs unbounded) where English uses one form and relies on context. This is the "narrate past events distinguishing completed actions from background" capability.
mistake: the central B1 challenge; English's simple past collapses this distinction, so learners must relearn it as aspect, not tense.
source: Eaquals "alternance" A2, "temps du passé dans le récit" B1

title: Plus-que-parfait
explanation: imparfait of avoir/être + past participle = "had done" (a past before the past). Essential for reported speech and si-clauses.

examples.native: Il avait déjà mangé quand je suis arrivé.
examples.gloss: He had already eaten when I arrived.

bridge_note: Documented level split: Eaquals/Beacco place plus-que-parfait at B1; Kwiziq at B2. Recommendation: introduce at B1, consolidate at B2.
mistake: using passé composé where anteriority is needed.

title: Passé simple (recognition only)
explanation: The literary/historical narrative past — learners need to recognize it (il fut, il eut, il alla, il fit), not produce it.

examples.native: Il naquit en 1802 et mourut en 1885.
examples.gloss: He was born in 1802 and died in 1885.

source: Kwiziq B2–C1; a claim that Eaquals surveyed teachers and rejected teaching it earlier (citing a ~26% figure) appears in the source doc's prose but could not be traced to a specific URL or confirmed independently

title: Futur simple

title: Conditionnel présent
explanation: Future stem + imparfait endings. Uses: politeness, wishes, hypothesis, "future-in-the-past."
bridge_note: the conditional is literally "future + past" morphology — a Romance innovation ("infinitive + habēbam") expressing a future seen from a past/hypothetical vantage.
mistake: confusing the near-identical spellings of je parlerai (futur, "I will") and je parlerais (conditionnel, "I would") — a classic homophone trap.

title: Conditionnel passé
explanation: conditionnel of avoir/être + participle = "would have."

examples.gloss: I would have liked to come.
She would have left earlier (note être agreement).

mistake: "J'aurais aller" ✗ (participle needed, not infinitive).

title: Futur antérieur
explanation: futur of avoir/être + participle = "will have done."

examples.gloss: When you arrive, I'll have finished.

mistake: using the simple future where anteriority is meant.

title: The three si-clause types
explanation: French has three parallel si-constructions for hypotheticals, each pairing a specific tense in the si clause with a specific tense in the result clause: si + present for real/possible conditions, si + imperfect for present-unreal conditions (paired with the present conditional), and si + pluperfect for past-unreal conditions (paired with the past conditional). In practice, spoken French also freely mixes plus-que-parfait with the present conditional when a hypothetical past condition has a present-time consequence (Si tu avais étudié, tu aurais un meilleur travail aujourd'hui — "If you had studied, you'd have a better job today"); the three matched pairs above are the clean textbook pattern, but real usage sometimes crosses type 2 and type 3 depending on when the result is meant to hold.
long_form:
The conditional mood that anchors types 2 and 3 doesn't exist in Latin at all as a distinct category — which is a genuinely striking fact once you notice it, because French treats the conditional as such a basic, everyday mood that it's easy to assume it's as old as the language itself. It isn't. The conditional is a Romance-era innovation, built during the transition from Vulgar Latin to Old French out of a periphrasis: the infinitive of the main verb plus a form of avoir's imperfect (habebam, "I had" or "I was to"), fused together over time into a single word. That's also, not coincidentally, exactly how the futur simple was built, just with avoir's present instead of its imperfect (infinitive + habeo, "I have"). Which is why je parlerai (I will speak) and je parlerais (I would speak) aren't just similar-looking by accident — they're morphological siblings sharing the same infinitive-plus-avoir skeleton, differing only in which tense of avoir got fused onto the end, present for simple certainty about the future, imperfect for a future viewed from a hypothetical or past vantage point. The conditional is, quite literally, "future-in-the-past" encoded directly into its own verb ending.

Once you see the conditional's real job — expressing a future stance taken from an unreal or past standpoint — the three-way si-system stops looking like three unrelated memorized patterns and starts looking like one consistent logic applied at three different levels of reality: a real, live possibility stays in ordinary tenses (si + présent); an imagined present that isn't real needs the imperfect in the si-clause paired with the "future-in-a-hypothetical-present" conditional in the result; and an imagined past that didn't happen needs the pluperfect paired with the "future-in-a-hypothetical-past" conditionnel passé. The si-clause itself, notably, never touches the conditional mood at all in any of the three types — it stays indicative (présent, imparfait, or plus-que-parfait), because French treats the hypothesis as a stated fact-pattern to reason from, reserving the conditional exclusively for the consequence that follows from it. That's the entire content behind the classroom chant "les si n'aiment pas les -rais" ("si's don't like -rais endings"): the rule isn't arbitrary, it's protecting a real division of labor between the clause that states the premise and the clause that draws the hypothetical conclusion.

English does essentially the same conceptual work with a completely different toolkit, periphrastic rather than a dedicated mood: "if X, Y will" / "if X did, Y would" / "if X had done, Y would have," shifting tense backward by one step as its own marker of unreality — and even preserves a fossilized subjunctive in "if I were," a genuine, if isolated, echo of the fact that English once also had a mood dedicated to unreal conditions before losing it almost everywhere else. Portuguese runs the identical three-tier logic with essentially the same tense values, but with one real point of interference for a bridge learner to watch for: Portuguese uses subjunctive forms inside its own se-clause (se eu tivesse, se eu for), where French insists on the plain indicative imperfect or pluperfect — so a Lusophone learner's instinct to reach for a subjunctive-feeling form in the si-clause itself is a transfer error waiting to happen, even though the overall three-way architecture transfers beautifully.

Two nuances round out the picture. First, real spoken French doesn't always respect the clean type-2/type-3 boundary the textbook draws: when a hypothetical past condition produces a consequence meant to hold in the present rather than the past, fluent speakers freely pair the plus-que-parfait si-clause with the present conditional rather than the past one (si tu avais étudié, tu aurais un meilleur travail aujourd'hui — "if you had studied, you'd have a better job today," the studying is past-hypothetical but the better job is a present-time consequence) — a genuine, common, and grammatical blend that a purely rule-based drill won't prepare a learner for. Second, si doesn't always mean "if" at all — the identical word also introduces indirect yes/no questions (elle demande si tu viens, "she asks whether you're coming"), a completely unrelated grammatical function that has nothing to do with hypotheticals or tense-pairing, and beginners sometimes get tangled trying to apply the si-clause tense rules to a sentence that isn't conditional in the first place.

examples.native: Type 1 (real): Si + présent → présent/futur/impératif. Si tu viens, je serai content
Type 2 (unreal present): Si + imparfait → conditionnel présent. Si j'étais riche, je voyagerais
Type 3 (unreal past): Si + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé. Si tu étais venu, tu aurais vu le spectacle

bridge_note: the si clause states the hypothesis in the indicative/imparfait; the conditional lives only in the consequence clause. English's "if I were" (an old subjunctive) becomes plain imparfait si j'étais — no special form.
mistake: THE cardinal error — putting futur or conditionnel directly after si ("Si je serais…" ✗). French teachers chant « Les si n'aiment pas les -rais » ("si's don't like -rais endings").
source: Eaquals sequences type 1 at A2/B1, type 2 at B1, type 3 at B2
