title: Subjonctif présent — formation
explanation: Stem from the ils form + -e/-es/-e/-ions/-iez/-ent; key irregulars (aille, soit, ait, fasse, puisse, sache, veuille).

examples.native: que je parle, que nous fassions, qu'il soit

bridge_note: the subjunctive marks non-factual/subjective content in a subordinate clause after que; French preserved the Latin mood robustly, unlike English which largely lost it.
mistake: trying to "translate" it — English has only a vestigial subjunctive ("that he be"), so learners don't feel the trigger.

title: Core triggers: il faut que, vouloir que, necessity/will
explanation: Verbs and expressions of necessity or will (il faut que, vouloir que) trigger the subjunctive in the clause that follows que, because they impose the speaker's will on an action that hasn't necessarily happened. This only applies when the subject changes between the two clauses; when the subject stays the same, French uses an infinitive instead (je veux venir, not je veux que je vienne).
long_form:
The subjunctive is inherited, not invented — Latin had a rich, fully productive subjunctive mood covering hypotheticals, wishes, polite commands, and purpose clauses, and French is one of the Romance languages that kept that mood as a normal, everyday piece of grammar rather than letting it wither. English took the opposite path: its own Old English subjunctive eroded almost to nothing, surviving today only in a handful of fossilized expressions ("if I were you," "God save the Queen," "I insist that he go" rather than "goes") that most English speakers can't consciously identify as subjunctive at all. That asymmetry is exactly why the subjunctive is documented as the "grammar plateau" separating B1 from B2 French learners: English speakers arrive with no working mental category for a mood that isn't about tense or fact, only habit and rote fossils, so the whole idea that a verb form can encode the speaker's stance toward an event — rather than simply when it happened — has to be built from nothing.

What makes il faut que and vouloir que a sound place to start building that category is that French's subjunctive usage is, in practice, heavily rule-based rather than purely semantic: a fixed inventory of governing verbs and expressions mechanically requires the subjunctive in whatever follows que, largely independent of whether the situation actually feels doubtful, hypothetical, or emotionally charged in the way older grammar books liked to claim. Il faut que tu partes doesn't feel uncertain at all — it's a flat statement of necessity — and yet it triggers the subjunctive just as reliably as an expression of genuine doubt does, because what actually matters isn't the emotional temperature of the sentence but whether the main clause presents the subordinate content as an established fact or as something the main clause's subject wants, requires, or is reacting to rather than simply reporting. That's a more accurate way to think about the mood than "subjunctive means unreality," and it's also why French teachers increasingly describe the mood in terms of memorized trigger lists rather than a single unifying meaning: the trigger-based description actually predicts real usage better.

For an English speaker this genuinely is closer to learning a new grammatical instinct than learning new vocabulary, precisely because there's no live, productive English subjunctive to draw an analogy from. Portuguese offers the opposite experience almost entirely: it preserves a subjunctive mood at least as robust and pervasive as French's, triggered by the same broad categories — necessity, volition, emotion, doubt — so a Lusophone learner typically already has stronger native intuition for when a subjunctive-shaped mental category should apply than an English-speaking classmate does, even before learning a single French verb ending. The challenge for that learner isn't discovering that the mood exists; it's mapping the two languages' trigger lists onto each other precisely, because they don't align perfectly — a mismatch covered directly by the exception where espérer que unexpectedly takes the indicative in French despite behaving like a desire verb in both languages elsewhere.

The most common structural mistake by far is the failure to swap to an infinitive when the subject doesn't actually change between the two clauses: English "I want him to come" maps naturally onto a subject-plus-infinitive shape that French simply doesn't have (there is no way to say "je veux lui venir"), while "I want to come" (same subject throughout) correctly collapses to je veux venir with no que and no subjunctive at all — the subjunctive-plus-que construction exists specifically to handle the case where the wanting and the wanted action have two different subjects, and reaching for it when the subject hasn't actually changed is the single most common way learners overuse the mood rather than underuse it. The deeper nuance, worth flagging even at this early trigger-list stage, is that the whole system is more gradient than a fixed list suggests: opinion verbs like penser and croire flip between indicative and subjunctive depending on whether they're affirmed or denied, showing that the underlying logic — does the main clause assert the subordinate content as fact, or hold it at arm's length — can apply to essentially any verb of assertion once its certainty or polarity changes, not just to the closed set of trigger words a beginner first memorizes.
mistake: using an infinitive across a change of subject ("Je veux qu'il venir" ✗); "Je veux que je…" (same subject → use infinitive: Je veux venir).
source: Eaquals; Kwiziq tags the il faut que / vouloir que + subjunctive lessons at B2

title: Triggers: emotion, doubt, subjective judgment
explanation: aimer que, être content que, avoir peur que, douter que, il est important que. One important exception: espérer que ("to hope that") takes the INDICATIVE, not the subjunctive, despite being a desire/emotion verb — unlike souhaiter que, which does trigger the subjunctive (je souhaite qu'il vienne).

examples.native: Je suis content que tu sois là.

examples.gloss: I hope he'll come. (indicative, not subjunctive — espérer is the exception)

mistake: assuming espérer que triggers the subjunctive by analogy with other hope/desire verbs ("J'espère qu'il vienne" is widely heard in casual speech but considered non-standard; the expected form is j'espère qu'il viendra/vient).

title: Opinion verbs: indicative when affirmative, subjunctive when negated/questioned
explanation: Opinion verbs like penser and croire take the indicative when stated affirmatively, since the speaker is asserting something as fact. Negating or questioning the same verb casts doubt on the claim, which flips the following clause to the subjunctive.

examples.native: Je pense qu'il est là. (indicative) BUT Je ne pense pas qu'il soit là. (subjunctive)

mistake: not flipping the mood under negation.

title: Subjunctive after conjunctions (bien que, pour que, avant que, jusqu'à ce que)
explanation: A fixed set of subordinating conjunctions — bien que, pour que, avant que, jusqu'à ce que — always require the subjunctive in the clause they introduce, regardless of what the main clause means. après que is a frequent exception in careful usage: despite looking like the others, it historically takes the indicative. As with il faut que/vouloir que, several of these have an infinitive alternative used when the subject doesn't change across clauses: avant de + infinitive, pour + infinitive, and sans + infinitive replace avant que/pour que/sans que + subjunctive when both clauses share a subject (il est parti avant de manger, not avant qu'il mange).

examples.native: Bien qu'il soit fatigué, il travaille.
Je t'explique pour que tu comprennes.
examples.gloss: I'm explaining so that you understand.

bridge_note: Portuguese draws the same line for concessive conjunctions — bien que + subjunctive corresponds closely to embora + subjuntivo — so the trigger-based logic transfers directly, even though the exact conjunction list and edge cases (like après que) differ.
mistake: using indicative after these; note après que historically takes the indicative; using the que + subjunctive form even when the subject is the same across both clauses, where the infinitive form is expected instead ("il est parti avant qu'il mange" ✗ when the subject is the same → avant de manger).

title: Subjonctif passé
explanation: subjunctive of avoir/être + participle = completed action in a subjunctive context.

examples.native: Je suis content que tu sois venu.

title: Subjonctif imparfait (recognition, foundational only)
explanation: Recognize forms like qu'il fût, qu'il eût in literary/formal texts; not for production. Flagged as recognition-only, foundational-C1.

examples.gloss: that he were, that he had (literary subjunctive imperfect, recognition only)

title: qui and que (simple relative pronouns)
explanation: qui = subject ("who/which"), que = direct object ("whom/which"). que elides to qu'; qui never does.
long_form:
Qui and que descend directly from a Latin pair, qui (nominative, the subject-marking case) and quem (accusative, the object-marking case) — and what's genuinely striking, once you know that, is that French kept this old case-based contrast as the organizing logic for its relative pronouns for centuries after it dismantled case marking almost everywhere else in the language. Nouns, adjectives, definite articles — all lost their Latin case endings as French developed, leaving word order to do the job case endings used to do. But the qui/que split survived, precisely because relative pronouns, like personal object pronouns discussed elsewhere in this curriculum, are frequent and grammatically load-bearing enough to resist a language's general drift toward simplification. A grammatical distinction can quietly outlive the very case system that originally motivated it, as long as the words carrying it are used constantly enough to stay fixed in speakers' memory as a pair rather than dissolving into a single all-purpose form.

The organizing principle itself — subject versus object, not any semantic property of the noun being replaced — is exactly what trips up English speakers, because English's relative pronoun system runs on a completely different axis: animacy. English chooses who/whom for people and which for things, largely regardless of whether that person or thing is the subject or object of the relative clause; French couldn't care less whether l'homme qui parle names a person or que je vois names a thing, and cares entirely about whether the pronoun is doing the subject's job or the object's. That's a genuine category mismatch, not just a vocabulary gap, which is why simply translating "who" as qui and "which" as que produces wrong answers roughly half the time — le livre qui est sur la table ("the book that is on the table," qui because livre is the subject of est) is exactly as correct as l'homme que je vois ("the man that I see," que because homme is the object of vois), even though English instinct would want "who" for the man and something else for the book.

Interestingly, English already possesses the role-neutral relative pronoun French is asking for — it's "that," which works for subjects and objects alike, for people and things alike ("the book that is on the table"; "the man that I see") — so the raw grammatical resource for thinking role-first rather than animacy-first already exists in English, it's just not the pronoun learners reach for by default. Portuguese, meanwhile, complicates the transfer from the other direction: its relative pronoun que is fully invariant for both subject and object roles (o livro que eu li, "the book that I read," object; o homem que fala, "the man who speaks," subject — the identical word, que, doing both jobs). That means a Lusophone learner isn't bringing over a habit that helps here; Portuguese under-differentiates exactly the distinction French requires, so learning qui versus que is acquiring a genuinely new grammatical contrast rather than transferring or unlearning an existing one.

Beyond the core who/which-versus-role confusion, the second persistent mistake is trying to drop the relative pronoun the way casual English allows ("the book I read," no connector at all) — French relative clauses can never omit qui or que, the connector is structurally obligatory every time, no matter how short or obvious the clause. A smaller, easy-to-miss trap sits in the two words' different behavior around vowels: que elides to qu' before any vowel sound (que + il becomes qu'il), while qui never elides under any circumstances, even directly before a vowel-initial verb — qui a dit ça? stays qui a, never contracting to qu'a in this relative/interrogative function, which matters because qu'a does exist in French as an entirely different fixed expression, making this one of the places where over-applying French's general elision habit produces a form that looks plausible but is simply wrong.

examples.native: L'homme qui parle est mon prof.
examples.gloss: The man who is speaking is my teacher.

examples.native: Le livre que je lis est bon.
examples.gloss: The book (that) I'm reading is good.

mistake: choosing by "who vs which" (English logic) instead of by grammatical role (subject vs object); dropping the relative pronoun (English can — "the book I read" — French cannot).

title: où (where/when) and dont (of which/whose)
explanation: dont replaces de + noun: "whose," "of which," "about which."

examples.native: l'homme dont la voiture est rouge
examples.gloss: the man whose car is red.

mistake: dont's word order (French keeps subject-verb: dont la voiture est…, not English "whose car…"); using que where dont is required by a de-verb (parler de → dont).

title: lequel/laquelle and preposition + relative
explanation: After a preposition, use lequel/laquelle/lesquels/lesquelles (contracting: auquel, duquel). For people, qui is also possible after a preposition.

examples.native: la table sur laquelle je travaille
examples.gloss: the table on which I work.
the friend with whom I travel.

mistake: stranding the preposition at the end (English habit — "the table I work on" ✗ literal).
source: Eaquals B2 "pronoms relatifs composés"; Kwiziq B2

title: ce qui / ce que / ce dont (indefinite relatives) and mise en relief
explanation: "What" (= the thing that); and cleft emphasis.

examples.native: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu dis.
examples.gloss: I don't understand what you say.

examples.native: Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est la musique.

mistake: using qu'est-ce que (a question form) inside a statement.

title: The passive voice (être + past participle + par/de)
explanation: Participle agrees with subject. Only verbs with a direct object can be passivized (unlike English, indirect objects cannot become passive subjects).
long_form:
Latin had a genuine synthetic passive voice — a whole dedicated set of verb endings, amor, amaris, amatur ("I am loved, you are loved, he/she is loved"), built directly into the verb the same way active endings were, with no separate auxiliary needed at all. That entire system was lost as spoken Latin's verb morphology simplified into the Romance languages, and French — like Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese — had to rebuild passive meaning analytically, from scratch, using être plus a past participle: essentially the exact same strategy English independently settled on with be plus past participle. This is a case of convergent grammatical evolution rather than shared inheritance or borrowing: two language families facing the same problem (how do you express "the letter was written" once your verb endings no longer distinguish active from passive) and arriving at structurally identical solutions. That convergence is also, refreshingly, why French and English passive syntax actually line up better than almost any other construction the two languages share — la lettre a été écrite par Marie maps onto "the letter was written by Marie" almost word for word, agent phrase and all.

The real divergence isn't the passive's shape, then, but a restriction on what it can promote to subject position. English readily passivizes an indirect object — "I was given a book," "she was told the news" — because English's object pronouns don't syntactically distinguish direct from indirect objects the sharp way French's do (compare je le vois, direct, with je lui parle, indirect: French keeps these grammatically separate at every level, including in the passive). French's être-passive can only ever promote a genuine direct object to subject position, which means "I was given a book" simply has no direct French passive translation at all — French speakers reach for on instead (on m'a donné un livre, literally "one gave me a book") or keep the indirect object pronoun active in some other construction. Portuguese shares this exact restriction — ser plus particípio is likewise limited to direct objects — so this particular constraint is a shared Romance inheritance, not a French idiosyncrasy, which means a Lusophone learner will find the restriction intuitive on arrival while an English speaker has to actively unlearn a habit their own grammar makes effortless.

There's a second, more idiomatic divergence layered on top of the structural one: French simply prefers the passive far less often than English does in everyday usage, especially for generic or habitual statements. Where English comfortably says "French is spoken here," French speakers gravitate toward the active on-construction (on parle français ici) as the natural, unmarked way to make an agentless general statement — the être-passive exists and is grammatical, but reaching for it in contexts like this tends to read as stiff or visibly "translated" rather than as native phrasing, a stylistic fact that goes beyond strict grammaticality and is easy to miss if you only learn the passive's mechanics without also learning when native speakers actually reach for it (there's a third alternative, too, the pronominal passive with se, that often sounds even more natural than either option for describing general facts and rules).

One nuance rarely surfaces until a learner has had real exposure to written French: the choice between par and de after a passive participle isn't free variation, it's carrying its own distinction. Par introduces a genuine agent performing a specific, identifiable action — la lettre a été écrite par Marie, Marie actually did the writing — while de tends to appear with more static, descriptive relationships, especially with verbs of covering, accompanying, or feeling (la montagne est couverte de neige, "the mountain is covered in snow," where snow isn't an agent performing an act of covering so much as a state the mountain is described as being in). Textbooks rarely spell this out at the point the passive is first introduced, but it's exactly the kind of distinction a learner starts noticing by ear once they've read enough real French to feel when par sounds wrong and de sounds right, or vice versa.

examples.native: La lettre a été écrite par Marie.
examples.gloss: The letter was written by Marie.

bridge_note: French prefers active on ("on parle français ici") where English reaches for the passive; the on-construction is the everyday alternative.
mistake: trying to passivize an indirect object ("I was given a book" has no direct French passive — French uses on m'a donné un livre).
source: Eaquals tags passive at B2; Elon.io's "Parcours B2" lists it as a headline B2 acquisition
branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative

title: Reported/indirect speech — present
explanation: Statements → que; yes/no questions → si; imperatives → de + infinitive.
mistake: keeping the interrogative inversion inside the reported clause ("Il demande viens-tu" ✗).
branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative

title: Reported speech in the past — concordance des temps
explanation: When the reporting verb is past, tenses shift back: présent→imparfait, passé composé→plus-que-parfait, futur→conditionnel; time words shift (demain→le lendemain, hier→la veille).

examples.native: « Je viendrai demain » → Il a dit qu'il viendrait le lendemain.
examples.gloss: He said he would come the next day.

mistake: not backshifting the tense or the time adverbs.
branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative

title: Gérondif (en + present participle)
explanation: Present participle = verb stem + -ant. En + -ant expresses simultaneity ("while ...-ing") or means ("by ...-ing"). The subject of the gérondif MUST be the main-clause subject.

examples.native: En arrivant, j'ai vu la lettre.
examples.gloss: On arriving, I saw the letter.

mistake: over-using it as an English "-ing" (French uses it far less; "I like swimming" = j'aime nager, an infinitive, not a participle).
branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative

title: Present participle & adjectif verbal
explanation: The bare participle (without en) can act adjectivally (agreeing) or verbally (invariable): une histoire amusante (adj., agrees) vs un enfant obéissant à ses parents (verbal, invariable).

examples.native: une histoire amusante / un enfant obéissant à ses parents
examples.gloss: an amusing story (adjective, agrees) / a child obedient to his parents (verbal, invariable)

mistake: agreeing the verbal participle.
branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative

title: Causative faire + infinitive
explanation: "To have/make something done." faire + infinitive is an unbreakable unit; nouns follow the infinitive, but ALL object pronouns go before faire, and the participle fait is invariable.

examples.gloss: I'm having it repaired by him.

examples.native: se faire + inf.: Il s'est fait couper les cheveux.

bridge_note: faire + infinitive fuses into one predicate, so the clitics attach to the whole unit at its front, exactly as they do to a simple verb.
mistake: placing pronouns before the infinitive ("Je fais la réparer" ✗); agreeing fait ("Elle s'est faite opérer" ✗ → fait).
source: Kwiziq/consensus B2; Elon.io "Parcours B2" lists the faire-causative among headline B2 acquisitions; Eaquals not separately tagged
branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative

title: Infinitive constructions: verbs + à / de / ø + infinitive
explanation: Some verbs take a bare infinitive (aimer, vouloir), some need à (commencer à, apprendre à), some need de (décider de, essayer de).

examples.native: J'ai décidé de partir. / Il a commencé à pleuvoir

mistake: wrong preposition — must be memorized per verb; this is a persistent B2 accuracy issue.
source: Eaquals A2 for basic infinitive structures, extended B1/B2
branch: Advanced Verb Structures: Passive, Reported Speech, Gérondif, Causative

title: tu vs vous
explanation: tu = singular familiar (friends, family, children, peers, animals); vous = formal singular AND all plurals.
long_form:
Sociolinguists have a name for the pattern French's tu/vous distinction belongs to: the "T/V distinction," coined directly from the Latin pronouns tu and vos in Roger Brown and Albert Gilman's influential 1960 study "The Pronouns of Power and Solidarity," which traced this exact phenomenon across dozens of European languages. The pattern's origin is genuinely political: in the late Roman Empire, the plural pronoun vos began to be used to address a single emperor, on the logic that an emperor who ruled jointly (or who was felt to embody the entire state) deserved to be addressed as though he were more than one person — a grammatical inflation of respect through grammatical plurality. That imperial habit spread outward across medieval Europe as a marker of social hierarchy generally, and French inherited and generalized it into the vous a commoner used toward anyone of higher status, eventually softening from a strict power marker into today's broader familiarity/formality axis that governs friends versus strangers as much as it once governed subjects versus kings.

French's relationship with this system is more politically charged than a modern textbook entry lets on: during the Revolution, the National Convention actually pushed to abolish vous altogether, mandating universal tu between citizens as a deliberate grammatical enactment of equality — the logic being that a truly equal society has no linguistic room for hierarchy, not even a pronoun's worth. The experiment didn't survive the fall of the Terror, and vous returned to ordinary use, but the episode is a genuinely telling data point about how much cultural and political weight French speakers have, at various points, invested in what looks from the outside like a purely mechanical grammatical choice.

English actually had this exact same system until surprisingly recently in linguistic-historical terms: "thou" was the intimate, singular form and "you" the polite, plural form, mapping onto tu/vous almost perfectly, before "thou" died out of ordinary use by roughly the 18th century, surviving only in religious and archaic registers — which produces the ironic modern effect that addressing God as "Thou" now reads as elevated and formal to English ears, even though "thou" was originally the intimate, familiar form and its disappearance from everyday speech is precisely why it now feels reserved for the most formal occasions imaginable. So an English speaker isn't learning an alien category here so much as relearning a distinction their own language once had and voluntarily gave up. Portuguese offers a richer, still-active comparison instead of a clean transfer: depending on region, Portuguese runs a three- or four-way system — tu, você, o senhor/a senhora, and regionally a fossilized vós — with você itself descending from a formal address, vossa mercê ("your mercy"), that has since drifted all the way to becoming the ordinary, unmarked pronoun of everyday address in Brazilian Portuguese. That's the T/V drift playing out on a different timeline and a different regional map than either French or English took, which makes it a genuinely rewarding comparison for a bridge learner to sit with rather than something that maps cleanly onto tu/vous.

The practical mistakes worth naming go beyond simple over-familiarity: choosing tu with a stranger or a superior reads as presumptuous, but the reverse — staying rigidly on vous with someone who has signaled, explicitly or through repeated informal cues, that they'd welcome the switch to tu — can itself read as coldness or a refusal of the relationship the other person is offering, which is exactly why French has dedicated verbs, tutoyer and vouvoyer, for the act of choosing (or renegotiating) this pronoun with someone; the choice is a live communicative act, not a fixed setting decided once and forgotten. A smaller structural nuance worth knowing: the "polite plural" vous addressing a single person still triggers a plural verb conjugation but, in careful usage, singular adjective agreement (vous êtes content, said to one man, keeps the adjective singular even though the verb form is vous's own) — a small grammatical tell that underneath its plural verb form, the polite vous is still, semantically, addressing exactly one person, unlike a genuine plural vous addressing several people at once (vous êtes contents).

examples.native: Tu viens ? (à un ami) / Vous venez ? (à un professeur)
examples.gloss: Are you coming? — to a friend / to a teacher (formal)

bridge_note: the "polite plural" vous is the medieval "royal you" — addressing one important person as many — a pan-Romance courtesy pattern.
mistake: tu to a stranger/superior (over-familiar); the verbs tutoyer/vouvoyer name the choice.

title: Register in negation: dropping ne
explanation: Spoken casual French routinely drops ne (je sais pas); formal/written French keeps it. Teach as register, not error.

examples.native: Je sais pas. (spoken) / Je ne sais pas. (formal)

title: Register in questions
explanation: Intonation questions = casual; est-ce que = neutral; inversion = formal/written. Same meaning, different register.

examples.native: Tu viens ? / Est-ce que tu viens ? / Viens-tu ?
examples.gloss: Are you coming? — casual / neutral / formal

title: on for nous
explanation: Colloquial "we" (on y va), impersonal "one/people" (on parle français ici), and passive-avoidance (on m'a dit).

examples.native: On y va ! / On parle français ici. / On m'a dit...
examples.gloss: Let's go! / People speak French here. / I was told... (lit. "one told me")

mistake: over-formal nous in casual speech; forgetting on takes a 3rd-singular verb but plural agreement of adjectives (on est contents).

title: Formal vs familiar vocabulary and structures
explanation: e.g., bosser (fam.) vs travailler; bouquin vs livre; slang and verlan awareness (recognition). Flagged as needing native-teacher curation.

examples.native: bosser (fam.) vs travailler / bouquin vs livre
examples.gloss: to work (casual) vs to work (neutral) / book (casual) vs book (neutral)

title: Shared architecture (positive transfer)
explanation: Both descend from Latin and share: two grammatical genders with agreeing articles/adjectives; definite/indefinite articles; conjugated verb systems with indicative, subjunctive, and conditional moods; tense/aspect distinctions; SVO order; and a large cognate learned vocabulary (nation/nação, information/informação, culture/cultura). A learner of one has a substantial head start on the other.

examples.gloss: nation, information, culture — cognates shared with Portuguese (a nação, a informação, a cultura)

title: Cognate grammar point — the subjunctive
explanation: Both languages use the subjunctive robustly after que for will, emotion, doubt, and after concessive conjunctions (Fr. bien que + subj. ≈ Pt. embora + conjuntivo). Divergence to flag: Portuguese has a living future subjunctive (quando eu for, se eu quiser) — a distinctively Ibero-Romance development preserving the Latin future-perfect/subjunctive-perfect after quando/se — with no French equivalent; French uses the present indicative after quand/si in those contexts. Portuguese also has a productive personal (inflected) infinitive (é importante nós estudarmos) that French entirely lacks; French must use que + subjunctive. Note terminology: Portugal calls it conjuntivo, Brazil subjuntivo.

examples.gloss: I have to leave. (French: present indicative after quand/si; Portuguese would use a future subjunctive in the equivalent quando/se clause)

title: Cognate grammar point — clitic (object) pronoun placement
explanation: Both have unstressed object pronouns. Major divergence: French fixes clitics BEFORE the conjugated verb in almost all cases (je le vois). European Portuguese has a three-way system — enclisis (after the verb, the default: vejo-o), proclisis (before, triggered by negation, wh-words, and certain conjunctions: não o vejo), and mesoclisis (inside the future/conditional: vê-lo-ei). Brazilian Portuguese generalizes proclisis in speech. A French speaker's instinct to front the clitic is correct for Portuguese only in the triggered (proclisis) cases and always wrong for the default enclitic case.

examples.gloss: I see him/it. (clitic fixed before the verb — contrast Portuguese’s default enclisis: vejo-o)

title: Cognate grammar point — compound tenses
explanation: Both build compound pasts with an auxiliary + past participle. Divergence: French splits the auxiliary between avoir and être (with subject agreement for être-verbs and reflexives); Portuguese uses ter (and rarely haver) as the sole auxiliary and does NOT alternate to a "be"-auxiliary for motion verbs. Also, French passé composé doubles as the everyday spoken past, whereas Portuguese's pretérito perfeito is a distinct simple form (falei), and the Portuguese pretérito perfeito composto (tenho falado) means "have been repeatedly doing," not a simple past — a genuine false-friend of tense.

examples.gloss: I spoke. / She arrived. (French splits the auxiliary avoir/être; Portuguese uses ter for both)

title: False-friend traps (lexical, that derail grammar)
explanation: Watch cross-language faux amis that cause grammatical mis-selection. Within French for English speakers: actuellement = "currently" (not "actually"); assister à = "to attend" (not "assist"); attendre = "to wait for" (not "attend"); demander = "to ask" (not "demand"); passer un examen = "to take" (not pass) an exam; sensible = "sensitive"; librairie = "bookshop" (not library). Across French↔Portuguese, the shared Latin stock produces both true cognates and traps, and gender can differ on cognate nouns (a persistent transfer error documented in French-Portuguese translation studies), so gender should never be assumed to transfer.

examples.gloss: He attends the meeting. (assister à = "to attend," not "to assist" — a false friend)

title: Il y a (there is/are) — the existential construction
explanation: Il y a is French's all-purpose "there is/are," built from the impersonal il + y ("there") + a ("has") — literally "it there has." It never changes for the noun that follows (no agreement, no plural verb), and the same phrase also means "ago" when it follows a duration.

examples.native: Il y a des enfants dans le jardin.
examples.gloss: There are children in the garden.

examples.native: Il y a trois ans, j'habitais à Lyon.
examples.gloss: Three years ago, I was living in Lyon.

bridge_note: Portuguese's equivalent, há (from haver), works the same impersonal, invariable way (há um problema, há três anos) — a rare case where the two languages line up almost exactly, unlike most existential constructions.
mistake: conjugating il y a for number ("il y ont des enfants" ✗ — it never changes, even before a plural noun); confusing this "ago" use with depuis, which needs the present tense for an action still ongoing (see Time & Duration Expressions).

title: Prepositions with place names (en France, au Japon, à Paris)
explanation: The preposition for "to/in" a place depends on the place's gender and number, not on a single general rule: à before cities, en before feminine countries (and masculine countries starting with a vowel), au before masculine countries, aux before plural-named countries. Most country names ending in -e are feminine (la France, la Chine); most others are masculine (le Japon, le Canada) — with well-known exceptions (le Mexique).

examples.native: Elle habite en France. / Il travaille au Japon.
examples.gloss: She lives in France. / He works in Japan.
They're traveling to the United States.

bridge_note: Portuguese uses a similarly gender-driven system (na França, no Japão), but the genders don't always match French's — a cognate country name can carry a different grammatical gender in the two languages, so the pattern transfers but each country's gender still has to be checked individually.
mistake: defaulting to à for every place ("à France" ✗ → en France); guessing gender wrong for countries with irregular gender (le Mexique, not *la Mexique).

title: dans vs en (time until vs. time to complete)
explanation: dans + a duration means "in/after X time" — a future point counted from now (dans dix minutes = ten minutes from now). en + a duration measures how long an action takes to complete (en dix minutes = within a ten-minute span, start to finish). English "in" covers both, which is exactly why English speakers reach for the wrong one.

examples.gloss: I'll be back in an hour (from now).

examples.native: J'ai fini le rapport en une heure.
examples.gloss: I finished the report in an hour (it took an hour).

bridge_note: Portuguese draws a comparable line (daqui a uma hora for a future point vs em uma hora for duration-to-complete), so the underlying logic transfers even though the prepositions don't map word-for-word.
mistake: using en for a future point ("Je reviens en une heure" ✗ when you mean "an hour from now"); using dans for elapsed duration.

title: depuis, pendant, and il y a (que) for duration
explanation: depuis + present tense expresses an action that started in the past and is STILL going on now — where English switches to a perfect tense ("I have been living here for three years" = j'habite ici depuis trois ans, present tense, not a past tense). pendant states a bounded duration for a completed or habitual action, with no claim about "still going on." depuis and il y a … que / ça fait … que are interchangeable for the "still ongoing" meaning, just with different word order.

examples.gloss: I've been living here for three years (and still do).

examples.native: J'ai travaillé pendant trois ans à Lyon.
examples.gloss: I worked in Lyon for three years (a finished period).

examples.native: Il y a trois ans que j'habite ici. / Ça fait trois ans que j'habite ici.
examples.gloss: I've been living here for three years.

bridge_note: This is a genuine French/Portuguese-vs-English trap: Portuguese also keeps the present for an ongoing duration (moro aqui há três anos / faz três anos que moro aqui), so the depuis-logic transfers well from Portuguese, even though English grammar pulls in the opposite direction.
mistake: translating "have been doing" literally into a French compound past ("J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans" ✗ for an action still ongoing — French wants the present: j'habite ici depuis trois ans); using pendant where the action is still continuing.

title: Adverb placement in compound tenses (déjà, bien, encore, souvent between avoir/être and the participle)
explanation: Short, high-frequency adverbs of time, quantity, and manner — déjà, bien, encore, toujours, souvent, presque, trop, beaucoup — normally slide inside the compound tense, between the conjugated auxiliary and the past participle, not after the participle the way English puts them after the main verb.

examples.gloss: I've already eaten. (not: J'ai mangé déjà ✗)

mistake: placing the adverb after the participle by analogy with English word order ("J'ai mangé déjà" ✗, "Il a fini déjà" ✗); note that longer -ment adverbs of manner (rapidement, calmement) and most place/time adverbs (hier, ici, demain) instead follow the participle or sit at the sentence edge, so this rule is specifically for the short high-frequency set, not adverbs in general.

title: Indefinite adjectives and pronouns (chaque/chacun, quelque(s), plusieurs, certain(e)s)
explanation: chaque ("each") is an adjective and never takes a plural; its pronoun counterpart chacun(e) stands alone. quelque(s) ("some/a few") is an adjective agreeing in number only. plusieurs ("several") and certain(e)s ("certain/some") are inherently plural, and certain(e)s additionally agrees in gender.

examples.native: Chaque étudiant a son propre livre. Chacun a le sien.
examples.gloss: Each student has their own book. Each one has theirs.

examples.native: J'ai quelques questions. Plusieurs personnes sont venues.
examples.gloss: I have a few questions. Several people came.

bridge_note: Portuguese's cada ("each") is likewise invariable for both gender and number (cada aluno, cada aluna), so the "never pluralizes" instinct transfers directly from chaque; but Portuguese has no one-word equivalent to plusieurs, typically using vários/várias instead, which does agree in gender unlike French's plusieurs.
mistake: pluralizing chaque ("chaques étudiants" ✗ — it's invariable for number, always singular); confusing quelque (adjective, before a noun) with quelqu'un (pronoun, "someone").

title: tout / toute / tous / toutes — adjective, pronoun, and invariable adverb
explanation: tout changes function and agreement depending on its role. As an adjective meaning "all/every," it agrees normally (tout le monde, toute la classe, tous les jours, toutes les filles). As a pronoun meaning "everything/everyone," it's tout (singular) or tous/toutes (plural, with the -s of tous pronounced /tus/ unlike the adjective's silent -s). As an adverb meaning "completely/very," it's normally invariable (tout content) — EXCEPT before a feminine adjective that starts with a consonant or aspirate h, where it agrees for euphony (elle est toute contente, but elle est tout heureuse stays invariable because heureuse starts with a vowel sound).

examples.native: Tous les jours, je cours. Tout va bien.
examples.gloss: Every day, I run. Everything's fine.
She's completely happy. (invariable: heureuse starts with a vowel sound)
She's completely pleased. (agrees: contente starts with a consonant)

bridge_note: Portuguese's tudo/todo(a)(s) splits along a similar adjective/pronoun line (todo o mundo vs tudo bem), but Portuguese has no equivalent to the French adverbial tout at all, so this specific euphonic-agreement exception is a purely French wrinkle with no Portuguese shortcut.
mistake: treating tout as always invariable when used as an adverb (missing the feminine-consonant agreement exception); mispronouncing the pronoun tous as silent -s (it's the one context where the final -s of tous IS pronounced).

title: Verbs with a "reversed" subject (manquer, plaire)
explanation: A small set of common verbs — manquer (to miss), plaire (to please/like), and suffire (to be enough) — put the French grammatical subject where English would put the object, and vice versa. "I miss you" is really "you are lacking to me": tu me manques, with tu as the subject of manquer and me as the indirect object. Getting the pronoun order and verb agreement right requires thinking in French logic, not translating English word for word.

examples.gloss: I miss you. (literally: you are lacking to me)
I like this movie. (literally: this movie pleases me)
I miss my friends. (manquent agrees with mes amis, the grammatical subject)

bridge_note: Portuguese's equivalents split: faltar mirrors French exactly (Tu me faltas = "I miss you," the same reversed logic as manquer), but gostar de reverses back to a normal subject-verb-object pattern (eu gosto deste filme, "I like this film," with "I" as the ordinary subject) — so plaire's reversed logic does NOT transfer from gostar, even though manquer/faltar's does.
mistake: translating word-for-word and swapping the roles ("Je manque toi" ✗ for "I miss you"); forgetting the verb must agree with the person/thing doing the missing/pleasing, not with the English subject.

title: Exclamative constructions (que, comme, qu'est-ce que + clause)
explanation: French turns a statement into an exclamation with que, comme, or qu'est-ce que placed at the front of the clause — all roughly "how...!" or "what a...!" — with no inversion and no change to the clause's normal word order. quel(le)(s) is used instead directly in front of a noun, agreeing like the question word it doubles as.

examples.gloss: It's so cold! (lit. How it makes cold!)

bridge_note: Portuguese uses the same que/como pattern for exclamations (Que lindo!, Como está frio!), so the construction transfers almost word for word from Portuguese — one of the more forgiving corners of French syntax for a Lusophone learner.
mistake: inverting subject and verb as if it were a question ("Est-ce beau !" ✗ is a question, not an exclamation); using quel with a full clause instead of directly before a noun (quel belongs in quelle bonne idée !, not in front of an adjective clause).

title: The pronominal (reflexive) passive: se + verb for generic statements
explanation: Alongside the être + participle passive and the active on-construction, French has a third passive-avoidance strategy: a reflexive verb used impersonally to state what "is done" to something as a general fact or rule, not a one-time event with a named agent. It's especially common for describing how things are used, said, sold, or eaten in general.

examples.gloss: That's not said / You don't say that.

examples.native: Le vin blanc se boit frais.
Les billets se vendent en ligne.

bridge_note: Portuguese has the identical strategy — the reflexive passive with se (Vende-se vinho / O vinho branco bebe-se fresco) — making this one of the most directly transferable constructions between the two languages, right down to the impersonal, agent-less use.
mistake: reaching for the être + participle passive for general/habitual statements where French prefers this reflexive form ("Le vin blanc est bu frais" reads like a translated sentence, not natural French); trying to add a named agent to it (this construction has no par phrase — for a specific agent, use the être-passive or on instead).
